newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australian engineering construction boom seen.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australian engineering construction boom seen.

text.p: Australia's A$14 billion engineering construction industry is set for its strongest sustained boom period for at least the last 25 years, a study released by economic consultant BIS Shrapnel on Monday said.
The study, Engineering Construction in Australia 1996-2011, said a surge in private sector funding would underpin the boom.
"The next four years will be strongest period to date for private infrastructure activity with major projects of all types," the study's principal author, Nigel Hatcher, said in a statement.
The report said it expected private sector engineering construction to be worth about A$5.3 billion by 1998/99, up from A$2.8 billion in 1992/93.
Hatcher said private road construction would be particularly strong, boosted by the A$1.7 billion City Link project in Melbourne.
There would also be a major phase of investment in private electricity and pipelines, he said.
"Also boosting private work will be a major boom in mining and minerals processing investment, which will peak higher and last longer than the previous boom of the early 1980s," he said.
"Investment in both mining and secondary processing will increase sharply from already strong levels, while an upsurge in oil and gas field development is expected from 1997/98."

Hatcher said public sector-funded engineering construction would decline marginally over the next three years as a result of government cut-backs and as state-owned telecommunications carrier Telstra winds down its cable roll-out.
However, the impact would be partly offset by construction of Olympic Games facilities in Sydney and other state government programmes.
Hatcher said overall engineering construction grew 25 percent in the five years to 1995/96 and was expected to remain at the current record levels for four more years.

But he said the industry was expected to decline substantially from 2000/01 as an oversupply of some minerals emerged and as the private infrastructure sector became more subdued as a result of a weaker economy.
